name: Hideo Nomo
status: Retired as a player since July 2008. Today (Nov 2026, age 58) he works for the San Diego Padres in the USA: the club's front-office page lists him as 'Special Assistant, Baseball Operations'. In Japan he heads the non-profit NOMO Baseball Club. In November 2026 he was inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame in Los Angeles with its first 'Sports Pioneer Medal'. Where he lives is not confirmed by any reliable source.
summary: Japanese pitcher with the twisting 'Tornado' windup. In January 1995, at 26, he 'retired' from the Kintetsu Buffaloes to get out of his Japanese contract, signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers and became the first Japanese player to move to Major League Baseball (MLB) for good. He was called a traitor at home, then won Rookie of the Year. The route was planned with agent Don Nomura. Every Japanese major leaguer since has walked through the door he reopened.
tiles: MLB no-hitters (1996 and 2001), one in each league
NL Rookie of the Year and All-Star Game starter

quick_facts: Starting pitcher, right-handed. Known for the 'Tornado' windup and the forkball (a pitch that drops sharply)
Kintetsu Buffaloes 1990 to 1994: 78 wins, 46 losses, 1,204 strikeouts
1995 to 2008, 7 teams (Dodgers twice): 123 wins, 109 losses, ERA 4.24, 1,918 strikeouts
201 wins and 3,122 strikeouts (my addition of the two tables below)

Almost. Masanori Murakami pitched for the San Francisco Giants in 1964 and 1965, so Nomo was the SECOND Japanese major leaguer. He was the first in 30 years and the first to leave Japan for good against his club's wishes.
Don Nomura (confirmed). Agent after 1998: not confirmed
Silver medal at the 1988 Seoul Olympics (baseball was a demonstration sport). Never played in the World Baseball Classic
Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame 2014 (first year on the ballot). Cooperstown (USA): 1.1% of votes in 2014, dropped from the ballot
San Diego Padres front office (since Feb 2016); head of NOMO Baseball Club (founded 2003)
seasons_note: Source: Baseball-Reference (MLB page for 1995 to 2008, register page for Japan 1990 to 1994). ERA = earned run average, the runs a pitcher gives up per 9 innings; lower is better. Innings like '191.1' mean 191 and one third. I added every row: Japan gives 78 wins, 46 losses, 1,204 strikeouts; MLB gives 123 wins, 109 losses, 1,918 strikeouts. Both match the official career lines. He did not pitch in MLB in 2006 or 2007 (minor leagues and Venezuelan winter ball only). The Japan rows could not be cross-checked on NPB's own site.

timeline.event: Born 31 August in Osaka, into a working-class family. His father is described as a former fisherman who became a postal worker.
Starts twisting his body to throw harder as a boy. His father tells him to throw with his whole body.
Not wanted by the famous baseball high schools (Kindai Fuzoku is the one named). Enters Seijo Industrial High School, an ordinary public school.
Pitches a perfect game (no batter reaches base) in the Osaka summer tournament. Gets little press. Never reaches Koshien, the national high school tournament.
No pro team drafts him. Joins the company team Shin-Nittetsu Sakai (Nippon Steel). Learns the forkball there.
Silver medal with Japan at the Seoul Olympics (baseball was a demonstration sport).
A record 8 teams pick him first in the draft. Kintetsu wins the lottery. He signs on condition that the club will not change his pitching form.
Rookie season: 18 wins, 287 strikeouts. Wins MVP, the Sawamura Award (best starting pitcher), Rookie of the Year and the pitching triple crown.
Leads the Pacific League in wins and strikeouts four years in a row, under easygoing manager Akira Ogi (to 1992).
💍 Marries Kikuko Morimoto in his second year with Kintetsu (exact day not confirmed). They met when he was a company-team pitcher and she was a cheerleader for a rival company team, Toshiba.
👶 First son, Takahiro, born (year worked out from his reported ages; exact day not confirmed). A second son was born later; his details are private.
Keishi Suzuki, a 317-win legend with old-school ideas (throw more, run more), becomes manager. Friction begins.
Sore shoulder. On 1 July he throws 191 pitches and walks 16 in one complete game. Season ends early at 8 wins, 7 losses. Tells teammate Masato Yoshii he is going to America. Meets agent Don Nomura.

9 Dec: the Japanese commissioner's office confirms by fax that a 'voluntarily retired' player is only tied to his old club inside Japan. 13 Dec: he asks Kintetsu for a multi-year contract with Nomura at his side; the club throws Nomura out and refuses.
9 Jan: announces voluntary retirement and his plan to play in MLB. Kintetsu takes its flag down before the press conference. Called a traitor and an ingrate in Japan.
13 Feb: signs a minor-league contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers, with a $2 million signing bonus, after meeting owner Peter O'Malley.
2 May: MLB debut. Starts the All-Star Game in July. 13 wins, 236 strikeouts (best in the National League), Rookie of the Year. 'Nomomania' in both countries.
17 Sept: no-hitter at Coors Field in Denver, the hardest park for pitchers. Still the only one ever thrown there.
Struggles (2 wins, 7 losses). Asks the Dodgers for a change of team through Nomura; traded to the New York Mets on 4 June.
Released by the Mets, minor leagues with the Cubs, then 12 wins for Milwaukee. Detroit in 2000.
4 April: second no-hitter, for Boston at Baltimore, in his first game for the team. Leads the American League in strikeouts (220).
Back with the Dodgers: 16 wins in each season. In 2003 founds NOMO Baseball Club in Sakai for young players with nowhere to play. Shoulder surgery in October 2003.
Never the same after surgery (ERA 8.25 in 2004). 15 June 2005: 200th win of his Japan + USA career, with Tampa Bay. Released in July.
Refuses to quit: minor leagues with the White Sox, elbow rehab, then winter ball in Venezuela in late 2007.
Makes the Kansas City Royals in April, pitches 3 games, is released. 17 July: retirement announced, with no press conference and no farewell game.
Short coaching and adviser jobs with Orix and Hiroshima in Japan; starts TV commentary; starts taking a Japanese junior team to play in California.
NOMO Baseball Club moves from Sakai to Toyooka, Hyogo.
Elected to the Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame in his first year on the ballot. In the USA he gets only 6 votes (1.1%) for Cooperstown.
11 Feb: joins the San Diego Padres as Advisor, Baseball Operations.
30 years since his debut. Ichiro thanks him in his Hall of Fame speech (27 July). Throws the ceremonial first pitch before World Series Game 3 at Dodger Stadium (27 Oct).
Still with the Padres. Appears at Seibu veteran Takumi Kuriyama's retirement ceremony in Japan (30 Aug). Inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame in Los Angeles with its first Sports Pioneer Medal (Nov).

No-hitter at Camden Yards, Baltimore (Red Sox). Still the only one in that park

Japan: most wins and most strikeouts in the Pacific League, four years in a row
200th combined win in Japan and the USA
Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame, first year on the ballot; youngest inductee up to then
Asian Hall of Fame (Los Angeles), first 'Sports Pioneer Medal'

leadership_intro: Short answer: he was stubborn about a very small number of things (his pitching form, how to care for his arm, and where he wanted to play) and flexible about almost everything else, including money and comfort. Each time, he first proved the point with results, and he let other people do the talking. Six patterns show up again and again. The 'honest view' below shows what it cost.

leadership.title: He never let anyone change the Tornado
leadership.simple: From boyhood he twisted his back to the batter to throw harder. Scouts and coaches said it would never work. He kept it, and wherever a coach left it alone he gave everything back.
evidence: According to Robert Whiting, he began twisting as a boy to throw harder and to impress his father. (The 'fifth grade' detail rests on one author.)
https://sabr.org/bioproject/person/hideo-nomo/
University and company scouts dismissed him; one line reported in Number: 'With that form, we won't take him.'
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/860808
A senior at his company team told him a man may keep one thing he never changes. He decided that for him it was the form. (One article, speaker not named.)
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/860808
He signed with Kintetsu on condition that the club would not alter his delivery (Whiting, via SABR).
https://sabr.org/bioproject/person/hideo-nomo/
Company-team manager Mitsushige Hamasaki says he saw the value of the twist early and recruited him anyway.
https://gendai.media/articles/-/43540

leadership.title: He treated his arm as something that wears out
leadership.simple: In 1990s Japan the common belief was 'throw more to get stronger'. He believed, as American teams already did, that a pitcher's shoulder is a consumable. This was the real root of the clash with manager Keishi Suzuki.
evidence: A beat writer who covered the team says Nomo arrived at 1994 spring camp with shoulder trouble and did not throw in the bullpen at first, while Suzuki demanded 200 to 300 practice pitches.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/861472?page=3
1 July 1994: a complete-game win with 16 walks and 191 pitches.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/865749?page=3
His innings fell from 243 in 1993 to 114 in 1994 as the shoulder broke down.
https://sabr.org/bioproject/person/hideo-nomo/
Teammates later said the 'Nomo hates practice' image was a misunderstanding caused by poor communication.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/866100

leadership.title: He chose the dream over the money, and took the risk himself
leadership.simple: He gave up a salary of about 140 million yen in Japan for a minor-league contract in the USA with no guarantee he would ever pitch in the majors.
evidence: Number's headline calls him the man who gave up 140 million yen and chose a salary of 9.8 million yen.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/860810
Dodgers general manager Fred Claire told Nomura a major-league contract had to be earned, so the deal was a minor-league one.
https://www.walteromalley.com/international/courageous-warrior-hideo-nomo-made-the-ultimate-leap-to-change-baseball/
In January 1995 Kintetsu offered incentives worth close to 100 million yen to stay. He refused.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/860810
Dodgers pitching coach Dave Wallace said he had everything to lose and nothing to gain (via SABR).
https://sabr.org/bioproject/person/hideo-nomo/

leadership.title: He let them talk, and answered on the mound
leadership.simple: While Japan called him a traitor, he did not argue back in public. He said almost nothing, went to America and pitched.
evidence: When Nomura worried about the attacks, Nomo shrugged and told him to let people talk (Whiting).
https://robertwhiting.substack.com/p/the-book-of-nomo-chapter-5-the-nomo
He later said he worried about daily life without English, but had no anxiety at all about pitching: 「全く不安がなかった」.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/844702
Dodgers owner Peter O'Malley said he had the heart of a lion.
https://www.walteromalley.com/international/courageous-warrior-hideo-nomo-made-the-ultimate-leap-to-change-baseball/
Manager Tommy Lasorda said he represented himself and Japan with class, dignity and character.
https://japantimes.co.jp/sports/2008/07/19/general/now-retired-nomo-made-huge-impact-on-baseball

leadership.title: He picked people, not just teams
leadership.simple: He was loyal to the few people who believed in him and worked hardest for them: manager Ogi, agent Nomura, owner O'Malley.
evidence: At his signing he said the other interested clubs did not have a Peter O'Malley.
https://www.walteromalley.com/international/courageous-warrior-hideo-nomo-made-the-ultimate-leap-to-change-baseball/
In the first Kintetsu meeting he insisted that Nomura come into the room with him.
https://bunshun.jp/articles/-/90543
A later manager, Phil Garner, noticed that he seemed to do well for people he liked (via SABR).
https://sabr.org/bioproject/person/hideo-nomo/
Under Ogi, who left him alone, he led the league in wins and strikeouts four years running.
https://www.baseball-reference.com/register/player.fcgi?id=nomo--001hid

leadership.title: He would not stop until his body made him
leadership.simple: After surgery and release he kept trying for three more years: minor leagues, rehab, winter ball in Venezuela, one last month with Kansas City at 39.
evidence: In Venezuela in 2007 he dropped the full windup because it strained his elbow, and kept pitching.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/857554
He made the Royals in April 2008 and said he was very happy to pitch in the majors again.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/857553
His retirement was announced through Don Nomura on 17 July 2008, with no press conference.
https://archives-new.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2008/Jul/17/br/hawaii80717061.html
Twelve years later he still said that if his body recovered he would want to play again.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/844702

honest_view: He did not leave by a door the league meant to be open. The 'voluntary retirement' route was legal, but many in Japan saw it as getting around the spirit of the rules. Kintetsu lost its best pitcher and received nothing.
The same stubbornness that people admire also hurt him. He stayed on the mound for 191 pitches out of pride, and his shoulder failed in 1994 and again in 2003.

Manager Keishi Suzuki deserves fairness. His methods were normal for his generation and had won him 317 games. The reporter who covered the feud now says the press, himself included, built up the 'manager against ace' story, and one teammate says Nomo wanted to keep pitching in the 191-pitch game.
He was hard on the media. An American writer called him a lousy interview, and Whiting reports he shut out an NHK crew for three years.

His later numbers are ordinary. After 1997 his ERA was above 4.00 in most seasons, and his MLB career ERA is 4.24. American Hall of Fame voters gave him 1.1%. His importance is what he opened, more than his totals.
'First Japanese major leaguer' is wrong. Masanori Murakami was first, in 1964. The accurate claim is: first in 30 years, and first to move for good.

My analysis: he was right about the things he was stubborn about (the form, arm care, his own ability), and he had expert help exactly where he was weak (rules, law, English). Stubbornness alone would not have got him out of Japan. The plan came from Don Nomura.

roots.title: A working-class Osaka home
roots.text: Born in Osaka in 1968. His father Shizuo is described as a former fisherman who became a postal worker; his mother worked part-time at a supermarket. He started by playing catch with his father at about age five.

roots.title: Where the twist came from
roots.text: His father told him to throw with his whole body, like the famous pitcher Minoru Murayama. The twist grew from there during elementary and junior high school. Whiting adds that he wanted to throw harder and impress his father.

roots.title: Turned away by the big schools
roots.text: He tried for a strong baseball high school (Kindai Fuzoku is the one named) and was not taken. He went to Seijo Industrial High School, a public school with no baseball fame, where the coaches did not touch his form.

roots.title: A perfect game nobody noticed
roots.text: In July 1985, as a second-year student, he pitched a perfect game in the Osaka summer tournament. The papers were busy with the stars of PL Gakuen. He lost 0-1 in the last 16 the next year and never played at Koshien.

roots.title: The company team that took a chance
roots.text: Manager Mitsushige Hamasaki of Shin-Nittetsu Sakai (Nippon Steel's team) had been asked by a Seijo coach to look at the boy. He says he promised to make him a first-round draft pick in three years.

roots.title: Learning the forkball
roots.text: He could not get a slider to work, so in his first company year he learned the forkball. Hamasaki says he taught it. Whiting says Nomo slept with a ball taped between two fingers to widen his grip.

roots.title: From outsider to Olympian in one year
roots.text: He was not in the first list of 30 candidates for the 1988 Seoul Olympic team. A coach who was there says he made the final 20 by improving through camps and the national company tournament, and that he never complained.

roots.title: The manager who left him alone
roots.text: At Kintetsu, manager Akira Ogi and pitching coach Toshio Kanbe did not touch the delivery and let him train his own way. Under them he won 18, 17 and 18 games in his first three seasons.

personal.event: Married Kikuko Morimoto, a former cheerleader for the Toshiba company baseball team, in his second year as a professional. Number Web gives the year only; the exact day is not confirmed.
First son, Takahiro, born. He was reported as 22 in January 2015 and 23 in September 2015, which fits 1992. Gossip sites give 24 February 1992; not confirmed by a newspaper.
Second son born. He is a private person, so no name or date is recorded here.
Founded NOMO Baseball Club in Sakai, Osaka, at his own cost, because company teams were closing and young players had nowhere to play.
Announced an agreement to move NOMO Baseball Club to Toyooka, Hyogo.
Elected to the Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame.

His eldest son Takahiro worked as an interpreter for the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters from January 2015 until the end of 2018, after graduating from a college near San Francisco. He went to international schools in Tokyo.
Joined the San Diego Padres front office.
Inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame (Class of 2026) in Los Angeles.

controversies.intro: No scandal was found: no report of a crime, doping, gambling or a personal-life scandal in Japanese or English (searched 21 Nov 2026). The controversies are all about HOW he left Japan and how he dealt with authority and the press. In most of them he was the target.

items.title: Called a traitor and an ingrate for leaving Japan
items.what: Media and baseball people attacked him. Whiting names Sadaharu Oh, Shigeo Nagashima and Senichi Hoshino among the critics, and reports that Yomiuri owner Tsuneo Watanabe called him and Nomura 'bad people'. He and Nomura received threatening calls and mail. Whiting also reports that his father did not speak to him for a time.
items.outcome: He said almost nothing and pitched. By the summer of 1995 he was an All-Star starter and a national hero in Japan. The US ambassador wrote that he had done more for the two countries' relations than the diplomats.

items.title: Clash with manager Keishi Suzuki
items.what: Suzuki believed in heavy throwing and running. Nomo believed in protecting the arm and training his own way. On 1 July 1994 he threw 191 pitches in one game. Some media called it punishment by the manager.
items.outcome: It ended with Nomo leaving. The reporter who covered it now says the press exaggerated the feud; teammate Yoshinori Sano says Nomo would have kept pitching out of pride anyway. Suzuki, now elderly, has not given his side recently.

items.title: Using the 'voluntary retirement' loophole
items.what: A retired player was only bound to his old club inside Japan. He and Nomura used this to leave without Kintetsu's permission. An NPB official complained of being tricked. Kintetsu got no payment.
items.outcome: Legal, and confirmed in writing by the Japanese commissioner's office beforehand. NPB then closed the route, and after two more Nomura cases (Irabu, Soriano) the posting system was created in December 1998.

items.title: Asked to leave the Dodgers
items.what: At 2 wins and 7 losses, booed at home and named in trade talks, he had Nomura ask the general manager for a change of team.
items.outcome: Designated for assignment (taken off the roster) on 1 June and traded to the New York Mets on 4 June. He returned to the Dodgers in 2002 and won 16 games twice.

items.title: Cold relations with the media
items.what: A New York writer called him a lousy interview with no sense of humour. Whiting reports he refused an NHK crew for three years after they ignored his request to keep their distance. A Japanese writer says the 1995 bashing made him wary of the press.
items.outcome: No incident of misconduct was found. Writers say he had softened by 2008.

items.title: Sponsors, business and NOMO Baseball Club
items.what: No sponsor deal or business matter that drew criticism was found, and nothing negative about NOMO Baseball Club. The Japanese search on the club was light.

deep_dives.title: The escape, step by step (1994 to 1995)
deep_dives.intro: Short version: Japanese players could not simply move to America. Nomura found one gap in the rules: a player who 'voluntarily retired' was only tied to his old club INSIDE Japan. So the plan was to make Kintetsu itself push Nomo into retirement, by asking for a contract the club was sure to refuse. It worked in under a month.

cells: Decided during 1994 that he wanted to go. Asked for the multi-year contract, signed the retirement form, and took the risk of a minor-league deal.
Found the clause, planned the 'ask for what they will refuse' strategy, was thrown out of the Kintetsu meeting, then talked to MLB clubs.
Checked the clause with Nomura on the US side. His own biography credits him with finding it; most accounts credit Nomura.
Went through Nomura's translation of the rules and the letters between the two leagues. Later became assistant general manager of the New York Yankees.
Refused to recognise an agent, refused the multi-year deal, and in the end handed over the retirement form.
Had the club call on the first day talks were allowed and closed the deal himself in his office.
Insisted on a minor-league contract: a big-league one had to be earned.
Nomo tells teammate Masato Yoshii he is going to America. He hears about Nomura through a mutual friend; they meet in late 1994 (Nomura says at a hotel or coffee shop) and talk about MLB.

After a question from the MLB commissioner's office, Yoshiaki Kanai of the Japanese commissioner's office replies by fax: a voluntarily retired player may only return to his former club within Japan. Nothing about abroad.

First contract meeting at the Miyako Hotel, Osaka. Nomura walks in with Nomo and is told to leave. Nomo asks for a multi-year contract; the club says no and offers a pay cut because of his shoulder. It lasts about 10 minutes.

Kintetsu offers incentives worth close to 100 million yen. He still refuses. Pitching coach Michio Sato tells the club to let him go. By Nomo's account he was in effect told 'then quit', said he would, and was handed the form.
Press conference: voluntary retirement and the move to the majors. The club flag is removed from the room first.
US press lists six interested clubs: Dodgers, Yankees, Mariners, Braves, Giants, Rockies.
Signs with the Dodgers at a hotel in Little Tokyo: minor-league contract, $2 million signing bonus (REPORTED).
MLB debut at San Francisco: 5 innings, 1 hit, 7 strikeouts, no runs. First pitch at 4:33 a.m. Tokyo time.

parts.heading: How big was the contract he asked Kintetsu for? Sources disagree
rows: Whiting: his 1994 salary doubled, on a three-year contract.
https://japanesebaseball.com/writers/display.gsp?id=34924
Yahoo Sports: a guaranteed multi-year deal of more than $5 million a season.
https://www.aol.com/star-pitcher-hideo-nomo-agent-195302074.html
JapanBall interview with Nomura: six years, $30 million.
https://japanball.com/articles-features/japanese-baseball-historical-profiles/negotiations-nomo-and-nomura-how-one-agent-changed-the-landscape-of-international-baseball/
Nomura's 2026 book: a term long enough to cover the roughly five seasons until free agency. No amount in the pages that could be read.
https://bunshun.jp/articles/-/90543
My note: all versions agree on the point that matters. It was a demand designed to be refused.

parts.heading: Lessons (my analysis)
rows: Read the actual rule, not what everyone 'knows' the rule is. The whole system rested on one word: 'active' players.
Get the other side's confirmation in writing BEFORE acting. The 9 December fax made the plan safe.
Let the other side close the door themselves. Kintetsu handed him the form; he did not have to break a contract.
The player has to be good enough to make the risk pay. Without the 1995 season this would be remembered as a failure.

deep_dives.title: The people around him: agent, gateway, money, mentors
deep_dives.intro: Short version: one agent (Don Nomura) planned the exit; one owner (Peter O'Malley) opened the American door; nobody knows publicly what the agent was paid.

cells: Don Nomura (団野村), based in Los Angeles. See his page under Agents.
Through a mutual friend, in late 1994. Nomo first asked about arm care and training in the USA.
The 1995 Dodgers signing and the June 1998 request to leave the Dodgers. His 2008 retirement was also announced through Nomura.
Not confirmed. No source says he left Nomura, and none names the agent for the later deals.

deep_dives.title: What changed after him
deep_dives.intro: Short version: his exit closed one door (the retirement loophole) and forced the two leagues to build a proper one (the posting system). About 74 Japanese-born players have now appeared in MLB.

cells: Masanori Murakami pitches for the San Francisco Giants. A fight over who owns his contract follows, and the leagues agree to keep their hands off each other's players. The door closes for 30 years.
Nomo leaves through the retirement loophole. NPB then rewrites the rule.
Mac Suzuki, who never played in NPB, debuts for Seattle.
Hideki Irabu refuses to be sent to San Diego and gets to the Yankees.
Alfonso Soriano 'retires' from Hiroshima; MLB declares him a free agent on 13 July.
The posting system is created: a Japanese club can offer a player to MLB teams and receive a fee.
Ichiro is posted to Seattle, the first star to use the system.
The system is revised twice: first a fee cap, then a fee based on the size of the contract.
Ohtani, Yamamoto, Sasaki, Murakami and others follow. About 74 Japanese-born MLB players as of mid-2026 (Wikipedia list; the O'Malley site says 'nearly 80').

The Dodgers twice gave out more than 100 press passes to Japanese media, and a US paper called him the best souvenir seller in the country (REPORTED, no dollar figures).

Opponent Ron Gant told him MLB had been saved by him.

money.changes_intro: Two baseball rules explain most of this table. First, a player new to Major League Baseball (MLB) has little say over his pay: for about his first three seasons the club sets it, close to the league minimum, and he can sell himself freely to any club only after six seasons. Second, once a pitcher is a free agent, clubs pay for health and recent results, often on one-year or minor-league deals, so an injury can cut pay very fast. (These rules are general background, not from one article.)

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: He led his league in wins and strikeouts in each of his first four seasons, so his pay rose every year.

changes.change: ⬇️ Salary down to about $109,000, plus a one-time $2 million signing bonus
changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: He left Japan by 'retiring'. His agents found that the rule only tied a retired player to his old team if he came back to Japanese baseball, not if he played abroad. Because he arrived as a newcomer on a minor-league contract, his yearly salary was near the MLB minimum. The bonus was the real payment. He chose the move over a higher Japanese salary.

changes.label: ESTIMATE; reason NOT confirmed
changes.why: He had just been Rookie of the Year. No source read explains the terms. My reading: he was still in the early years when the club controls pay, so the contract traded a modest price for three years of security, with the biggest amount in the last year.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: Injury and results. He had elbow surgery in late 1997 to remove bone chips, went 2 wins and 7 losses in 1998, and was traded to the Mets. The Mets released him after spring training 1999, the Cubs let him go after three minor-league starts, and he restarted with the Brewers from their minor leagues on a small contract.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: He won 12 games for the Brewers. He and the club could not agree on a long contract, so he became a free agent and signed with the Tigers for one year, $1.25 million plus bonuses for performance.

changes.change: ⬆️ Up: to $3.25 million (another table says $4.5 million)
changes.label: ESTIMATE; reason NOT confirmed
changes.why: One-year contract with the Red Sox, including a $1.25 million signing bonus. He had only 8 wins and 12 losses in 2000, but 181 strikeouts in 190 innings. No source read says why Boston paid more.

changes.change: ⬆️ Up: 2 years, $13.75 million, then $9 million in 2004 ($4.5M, $7.75M, $9M)
changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: His best bargaining moment. In 2001 he threw a no-hitter and led his league in strikeouts. He turned down Boston's 3 years and $19 million and returned to the Dodgers. The pay rose each year inside the contract, and he won 16 games in both 2002 and 2003. The $9 million for 2004 was the club's option year.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: His shoulder. He had rotator cuff surgery after 2003 and his fastball lost speed. In 2004 he won 4 and lost 11 with an 8.25 earned run average (runs allowed per nine innings; very high). The Dodgers released him, and he could only get a minor-league deal with the Devil Rays.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: Tampa Bay released him in mid-2005 after his 200th career win. A sore elbow ended his 2006 try with the White Sox, and he was out of MLB for two years. At 39 he signed a minor-league deal with the Royals, pitched three games in April 2008, was released, and retired that July.

fan_voices.intro: These are opinions from ordinary readers, not facts. They show how fans feel, and they are sometimes wrong. No usernames are kept and no comment is copied. Nothing here is used as a source for a fact.

samples.source: Yahoo! News Japan comments on the Nishi Sports article about his Asian Hall of Fame photo (17 Nov 2026)
samples.sample: The top 30 of 72 top-level reader comments in 'recommended' order (the page shows 89 including replies), read without logging in.
themes: He opened the door for everyone
Readers say later stars could try America only because he went first and succeeded, and that this matters more than his numbers. Several mention Ichiro thanking him in 2025.
Older readers recall him being called a traitor, the manager who doubted him, and how calm he stayed. One recalls him walking out alone after being released.
Watching the All-Star Game at school, visiting Dodger Stadium, his rare big smile. One says he was the only bright news in a dark year for Japan.
He saved MLB after the strike
Readers repeat the view that his starts brought American fans back in 1995.
The form was one of a kind
Nobody before or after threw like that; a pro who builds his own style and gets results has won.
Surprise at how much he has changed, mostly kindly. One comment guessing about his health was strongly disliked by other readers.
He deserves the American Hall of Fame; sad that no Japanese pro team has made him a pitching coach; hope he stays in baseball.
notes: The mood was overwhelmingly warm. I saw no comment criticising how he left Japan.
Several comments mix up small facts (for example which Japanese honour he holds). That is a reminder not to use comments as sources.
The counts overlap a little because some comments touch two themes.
